rv.q: It's exciting, even though you already know how it ends.
Junk melds a breadth of genres—crime story, tragedy, issue play, cautionary tale—into a fast-moving, broad-ranging social thriller.
That dash of moral and political ambiguity also injects tension into what might have been a didactic rehash of old journalism.
For greed, this cautionary tale points out, can be contagious, and that is a frightening message indeed.
But many will be left wondering if they really needed this dispiriting recap of the shift toward making money off money while building nothing but debt.

What it does do, in this slickly directed production directed by Doug Hughes, is capture the electric energy that fueled these aggressive acquisitions, along with the intoxicating sense of power that blinded the raiders to all other principles and values.
I esteem Mr. Akhtar for writing a big play about a big subject, but “Junk” is too slick to be fully satisfying.
“Risk” may be the watchword of its protagonist, the monomaniacal Robert Merkin (a miscast Steven Pasquale), yet “Junk” feels almost numbingly safe.
The play comes across less as a text emerging thrillingly to life than as a talking textbook.

In showing us how someone like Merkin operates, Ahktar reveals a painful truth: Our American love affair with ambitious mavericks exposes us to the machinations of those who would rob us blind — and we're often happy to help them do it.

Even with The Lincoln Center Review in hand, a copiously articulate companion publication available at the theatre for a dollar donation, Akhtar’s dense work simultaneously furrowed my brow and had me on the edge of my seat.
Cheers to Theater for producing this rangy, mordant new play and giving it the first-class production it deserves.

That such a love is misguided, blinding those afflicted with it to so much else in the world, contributes to the play’s melancholy chill, as does Akhtar’s awareness, pointed up in two key late scenes, that most of us will never feel or comprehend it.
Thanks to the smart script and staging, the result is top to bottom excellence for the small as well as major role players.
Fortunately, Akhtar, who won the Pulitzer for Disgraced, and his director Doug Hughes makes these complex maneuverings fascinating and exciting, if not entirely understandable.
Even while many of the characters are underdeveloped, 'Junk' is engrossing from start to finish.
The direction is lively, the effects powerful, and, while set in the ‘80s, the moral desert of the money cult and the latter-day “kings” in towers hold a very current punch.

NY1's Roma Torre filed the following review. The world of high finance is fodder for great drama. From the film "Wall Street" to the current series "Billions," it's easy to make villains out of the mercenary capitalists who'll do anything for an extra buck.
Akhtar sees to it that he's unlikely to be viewed as a sympathetic anti-hero; just a fascinating product of his time, surrounded by equally ruthless players of varying skills and nerves.

What we are left in the end is a real sense of the vulnerability of the global financial situation, which rests quite heavily on the Svengali-like influence of individual players, the old boy network, and the foolishness of those who are suckers for get-rich-quick schemes.
If there's little that feels unfamiliar or especially timely in 'Junk,' Akhtar has written a reasonably lucid primer
"Junk," at the Vivian Beaumont at Lincoln Center, is polished but lacks a satisfying punch.

What Junk suffers from—a familiar story, and an even more familiar band of character types—means that you don’t root for anyone, and neither do you despise anyone enough for their misdeeds, because the moral framework of the era and setting sanctioned those misdeeds.
As written by Akhtar, Junk is a mess and a shambles–as confusing as the recent history it means to recall.
Junk is a play that wants to be about everything and everyone, but ends up being about nothing and no one in particular.
With Akhtar's fidelity to finding the truth, Junk is another of his must-see plays exploring cultural mores.

Mr. Akhtar masterfully weaves together a collection of journalists, lawyers, businessmen, and traders to create a portrait of American wealth that is compelling, illuminating, and relevant all at once.
If the play doesn’t quite have the visceral impact of his previous plays (particularly Disgraced), Junk is a carefully-plotted and remarkably balanced piece of writing.
Junk will teach you that for some people, money is warfare.
Maybe you could say that in this tale of greed, we are given varying shades of black, with not a lot of differing tonal quality to look at.
The drama is brisk, but chilly, and entertaining…enough.
To others it will translate as an interesting and fast paced chronicle that is presented in a very impressive package.
He's done it with bold theatricality, in a sensational, large-scale production.
In many ways Junk is like a Shakespearean history play about war, complete with lies, betrayal, spies, sex, and blood, where words and actions can be twisted to mean something else.

cn.t: Critics are divided on Akhtar's ambitious 1980s Wall Street drama: some praise its timely relevance and breakneck pacing, while others find it overly familiar and more lecture than lived experience, with strong production values but limited emotional depth.

sg.ra: Thrust stage projects into the audience here, so front-center puts you directly in the actors' playing space with 180-degree eye contact. However, SeatPlan and JK's TheatreScene both warn the thrust's elevated downstage lip can obscure upstage action, and the shallow rake this close means you look up at performers working the far edge of the thrust.

At the middle of the thrust's semicircle, the stadium-style rake lifts you over heads in front while the curved row geometry keeps you square to the playing area — the thrust no longer feels side-on because you're on its central axis. SeatPlan, Headout, TickPick and Broadway Scene all converge on D-K center as the best sightlines in the house.

Sits on the central axis of the thrust so you see the three-sided staging in balance rather than from an angle. LCT's official chart confirms Row P has a dedicated step-up giving it elevation above Row O, and Headout lists L, P, O, K as the value-balance rows. At a thrust stage, back-center beats side-front because you read the full geometry of audience-wrapping blocking.

On a thrust stage, the far-side Orchestra seats end up looking ACROSS the playing space rather than at it — you see actors' profiles and often stare at the back of the thrust's far edge. SeatPlan: 'restricted views depending on staging.' JK's TheatreScene explicitly warns 'avoid the 4 or 5 seats closest to the wall.' BWW Forum thread 1082386 exists specifically because patrons worry about side-seat restriction at this venue.

The elevated Loge wraps the same semicircle as the Orchestra but 2 flights up (LCT: 30 steps), giving you the map-view of the thrust's three-sided blocking that's impossible from Orchestra. TickPick: 'Center, in the first three rows' is premium. SeatPlan confirms 'no bar or obstructions' at the front edge. For a thrust stage this is arguably a better seat than Orchestra for geometry-heavy stagings.

Only 5 rows exist in the Loge, so 'back Loge' is still close. TickPick: 'Rows D and E of Center Left and Center Right offer amazing views at a lower cost.' JK's TheatreScene paid $99 for similar seats and called them 'budget-friendly and worth every penny... view not appreciably different than the first few rows.' Elevated angle reads the thrust's three-sided blocking well even from slight side.

Compounds both weaknesses of a thrust-stage venue: you're on the far side of the semicircle AND at the back of the elevated tier, so the upstage portion of the thrust turns away from you. TickPick names Loge R Row E Seat 509 as the worked example: 'the rear end of the stage is going to be obstructed.' SeatPlan: 'Views from the Loge can feel distant, especially at the far sides.'
